Essay:

I think it is smart to ask more than one person before you make a big choice. I learned this from my cousin Dana. She is a nurse and last year she had to decide if she should quit her job and take a travel job in Arizona. She asked five people what they thought. At first I thought she was just wasting time because she was scared to pick. But then I saw how it helped her and I changed my mind.

The first reason is that one person doesn't know everything. Dana's mom told her to stay because the hospital has good benefits. That is true, but her mom never did a travel job before. A lady Dana works with did two of them. She told Dana stuff nobody else knew, like that you pay taxes on the housing money and that it's hard to make friends when you move every thirteen weeks. So each person only knew a part of it and Dana needed all the parts.

The second reason is that people want different things. Her mom wanted her to stay close to home. The recruiter gets paid extra if Dana signs up. Her best friend said she already missed her. They weren't lying, but they all had a reason to say what they said. If Dana only listened to the recruiter she would only hear the good stuff. When she heard all five she could tell what was a fact and what was just what that person wanted.

The third reason is when people who don't agree on anything all say the same thing, it is probably right. Almost everybody told Dana to read the part of the contract about canceling. She did, and it said the company could end her job with only one week of notice. She got them to change it to two weeks.

Asking people is not the same as letting them decide for you. Dana still picked for herself, and she didn't even do what her mom said. She took the job and kept her old license just in case. She came back eight months later with money saved and she was happy about it.

So one opinion is kind of like a guess. A lot of opinions is more like a map.
